records.name: IMPLEMENTED
records.text: An authorized caller creates a collection in StreamCore.createCollection. The Core assigns the collection identity and stores the artist address, supply information, and other collection state. Collection data is then set through setCollectionData. Creating the record does not mean minting has opened. Sale authorization, mint phases, executors, metadata, randomness, and economic configuration are separate pieces.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: IMPLEMENTED

records.name: IMPLEMENTED
records.text: For a 6529 drop, an offchain service prepares an EIP-712 authorization. The authorization binds the intended action to values such as chain, verifying contract, signer epoch, collection, payer, recipient, quantity, price, deadline, sale mode, and a replay-prevention identifier. The configured signer signs that payload. Solidity verifies the signature; Solidity does not calculate TDH or select the work. An authorization can drive a fixed-price execution or register an auction, depending on its sale mode.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: IMPLEMENTED

records.name: IMPLEMENTED
records.text: StreamCore.burn destroys the live ERC-721 ownership record. Normal tokenURI behavior no longer applies, but the protocol retains audit information about the burned token.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: IMPLEMENTED

records.name: OPEN FOR FEEDBACK
records.text: Reviewers should decide which metadata and provenance facts must remain reconstructable after burn, and whether retaining those facts creates any privacy or storage concerns.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: OPEN FOR FEEDBACK

records.text: The artist-facing inputs may include collection information, scripts, token data, images, attributes, dependency versions, a metadata mode, a randomness provider, supply limits, sale configuration, and revenue recipients. Different modules own different pieces.

records.text: The existence of a field in the protocol does not tell a reviewer who should be allowed to set it. The Roles and Trust page therefore treats every mutation as a separate permission question. Record-family checks are implemented in source, but the candidate's exact record-type admissions, live writer providers, grants, runtime code hashes, and rotation evidence remain unavailable.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: KNOWN LIMITATION

aliases: 14. Artwork finality is scheduled and executed
records.name: IMPLEMENTED

provenance.heading: IMPLEMENTED
headingPath: 14. Artwork finality is scheduled and executed

records.text: StreamArtworkFinalityRegistry supports a delayed finality process with scheduling, execution windows, cancellation or veto paths, component manifests, and terminal state. The delay is meant to create a visible ceremony rather than a surprise irreversible call. It also creates an operational obligation: participants must watch the schedule, verify the manifest, and act within the allowed window.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: IMPLEMENTED

records.name: Artwork lifecycle
records.text: This page follows one collection from creation to terminal finality. The purpose is to show where authority changes hands, which records become durable, and where a failed external service can stop progress.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle

records.name: 9. Metadata becomes available
records.text: tokenURI is produced from the collection's configured metadata mode and current token state. The renderer may use stored scripts, token data, dependency versions, images, attributes, and randomness output. “Available” and “final” are different. Metadata may be pending while randomness is unresolved. A later freeze can block mutations, but a frozen content hash still requires the corresponding bytes and execution environment to remain available.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: 9. Metadata becomes available

aliases: 10. Money follows one of several accounting lanes
records.name: CURRENTLY WIRED BASELINE

provenance.heading: CURRENTLY WIRED BASELINE
headingPath: 10. Money follows one of several accounting lanes

records.text: A paid fixed-price Drop keeps poster, protocol, and curator-reserve credits inside StreamDrops. It selects a token-level split first, then a collection-level split, then the contract default. The auction contract keeps a separate set of poster, protocol, curator, and bidder credits. These balances use pull withdrawals and must remain backed. The fixed-price accounting is in StreamDrops and creditFixedPriceProceeds. Auction proceeds are credited by AuctionContract.creditAuctionProceeds.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: CURRENTLY WIRED BASELINE

aliases: 10. Money follows one of several accounting lanes
records.name: SEPARATELY DEPLOYED FOUNDATION

provenance.heading: SEPARATELY DEPLOYED FOUNDATION
headingPath: 10. Money follows one of several accounting lanes

records.text: StreamRevenueResolver, StreamSplitFactory, StreamSplitWallet, and StreamPrimarySaleSettlement implement a different foundation that can resolve token, collection, and default revenue assignments. The rehearsal deploys those contracts, but the native Drop and Auction paths above do not call them.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: SEPARATELY DEPLOYED FOUNDATION

records.name: Questions for reviewers
records.text: Which state transitions need an artist signature in addition to governance? Which failures should automatically abort, and which should enter a recoverable pending state? Are Core freeze and artwork finality separated clearly enough? Which burn records must remain readable forever? What evidence must be published before a terminal finality action can be scheduled?
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: Questions for reviewers

records.name: 8. Randomness enters a lifecycle
records.text: If the collection requires randomness, minting creates a request bound to the token, collection, provider, and provider epoch. The provider may fulfill it, the post-processing step may fail, the request may be retried, or it may become stale.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: 8. Randomness enters a lifecycle

records.name: FAILURE BEHAVIOR
records.text: A pending live-token request can prevent metadata finality. A failed post-processing step can be retried only within the configured bounds. Provider migration is constrained while requests are pending. Burning before fulfillment follows its own recorded path; it is not treated as an ordinary live token. The Randomness page covers these states in detail.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: FAILURE BEHAVIOR

aliases: 15. Successor modules may take over replaceable duties
exactKeys: 15. Successor modules may take over replaceable duties
records.name: 15. Successor modules may take over replaceable duties

provenance.heading: 15. Successor modules may take over replaceable duties
headingPath: 15. Successor modules may take over replaceable duties

records.text: The long-term design records module identity, code hashes, interfaces, status, and successor relationships. A successor does not rewrite token history in the Core. It changes which replaceable module is recognized for a future duty. The critical review question is not merely “can this module be upgraded?” It is: who can register the successor, under what delay, with what evidence, and which old commitments remain binding?
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: 15. Successor modules may take over replaceable duties

records.name: 12. Supply is finalized
records.text: The collection can record final supply only after the relevant rules and delay have been satisfied. Final supply is one prerequisite for stronger terminal actions; it is not the same operation as freezing all collection metadata.
records.title: Artwork Lifecycle: 12. Supply is finalized
